summary: Two distinct measures are available: ABS domestic business employment (headcount) and IGEA full-time employment including FTEs and contractors. IGEA added nonresponding-studio estimates for FY2025; do not interpret that change as a consistent survey trend.

Abragames provides developer-workforce estimates for 2018, 2022 and 2023, including partners and workers at formal and informal developers. Outsourcing and foreign-worker figures exist only for changing employer samples. No newer verified national workforce observation was found by cutoff; the 2024 white paper repeats the 2023 estimate.

Annual Statistics Canada administrative ILUs cover 2015-2022, separate from periodic ESAC FTE estimates. The latest ESAC comparison is 35,250 revised FTEs in 2020-21 versus 34,010 in 2023-24. Contractor shares and 2015 immigration-status shares are survey-based, not comparable national citizenship counts.

CNG reports a selected major-listed-company personnel panel falling from 223,000 in 2021 to 205,800 in 2024. This is not verified as domestic game-only employment. The widely quoted 2018 national figure has undefined boundaries and cannot be joined to the panel.

CYGMA reports 1,438 people employed and paying taxes locally in 2019 and 4,320 in 2024. A 2025 report edition does not mean 2025 employment. Administrative coverage is broader than a pure games-publishing activity code.

Core developer/publisher employment 2015–2025 with association market estimates; broad ecosystem jobs excluded from preferred series. Latest 2026 edition has unresolved conflicting employment numbers and is retained separately.

Domestic game-production payroll FTE is verified for 2017–2022 in the 2024 edition. Earlier 2015–2017 and 2016–2019 vintages are retained separately because the population was redefined. The June 2026 Tableau workbook was downloaded and decoded: it covers film, TV and advertising only, with no games segment.

Annual 2015–2024 development-sector direct employment. External freelancers, foreign-origin workers and permanent-contract shares are separate; 2025 report was released in 2026 and forecasts are excluded.
Biennial studio employment 2016–2024; global totals include offices abroad. Domestic 2024 explicitly FTE and includes entrepreneurs. Sample nationality shares kept apart from national estimates.

EY reports direct employee FTE excluding independent workers: exact endpoints 6,674 in 2019 and 9,944 in 2024. The preferred 2019–2024 annual series uses the consistently rounded employment chart. Scope includes developers, publishers and technology suppliers. SNJV contract shares remain sample-only.

TIGA provides production-role FTE snapshots from 2016 to May 2024 and workforce counts including freelancers through September 2025. DCMS supplies a separate 2015-2025 annual jobs series, subject to substantial sampling uncertainty. Ukie surveys provide contractor and nationality shares; changing recruitment prevents treating share changes as national workforce changes.

An official 2024 ecosystem study published in October 2025 reports at least 2,112 talents at game developers/publishers. Its public author abstract does not establish a complete national census or precise headcount date. Wider estimates of hundreds of thousands of affected jobs are economic impact, not core employment.

Deloitte/GameIS reports about 4,000 workers in 2017 and 14,000 in 2021 across a broad ecosystem. Domestic-only employment is not established, and the company roster includes global offices and real-money gaming. These are context estimates, excluded from the domestic comparison.

Government-hosted EY report estimates around 66,000 gaming professionals, while a 2025 Primus report says 130,000 in more than 1,900 gaming companies. Their observation dates and gaming/RMG boundaries are not sufficiently defined for a national core comparison; no synthetic trend is created.

CESA estimates 58,000–83,000 workers in core game companies and about 200,000 including related industries, but the public 2025 release does not date its employment observation. It also includes console hardware in core. CEDEC provides sample-only worker-status composition for 2024 and 2025.

KOCCA reports 54,285 development/publishing workers in 2024, separately from 33,291 PC-cafe and arcade-venue workers. Verified annual core observations span 2015–2024. Repeated vintages show a one-person 2017 revision, retained explicitly.

DOSM occupation categories combine digital games with esports, and the inspected MDEC Southeast Asia studies report studio/respondent samples and salary distributions. No defensible national domestic development/publishing employment stock was verified; regional sample sizes are not country workforce totals.

Games Monitor gives 3, 834 jobs in 2018, 4, 560 in 2021 and 4, 291 in 2023. Most recent decline reflects companies moving outside the games definition. Includes self-employed specialists and applied games.
NFI/Virke reports employment in a changing respondent sample: 838 people and 813 FTE in 2024. Historical permanent/temporary employee counts are available, but not a national population series.

NZGDA annual survey observations span 2015-2025. Source units alternate between full-time employees, workers and FTEs, while respondents change. Later editions mention overseas staff. Keep snapshots and visa composition separate; no national index.

BOI reports more than 2,000 game-industry workers in an article postedJanuary 2018, but references to last year alongside Gamescom 2016 make the actual observation year ambiguous. The 2022 target of 4,000 is a forecast. More recent creative-economy/digital-interactive totals include other industries and are not a clean games workforce.

Game Industry Conference/PARP reports domestic game-production workforce snapshots of 12, 110 in 2021, 15, 290 in 2023 and 14, 568 in 2025, plus foreign-worker figures.2025 studio coverage changed; auxiliary services excluded.

RGDA snapshots show 6, 800 employees/collaborators in 2022, 6, 600 in 2023 and 6, 100 employees in 2024. Wording changed in 2025 release, so employee-only and collaborator-inclusive populations remain separate.
National estimates of 4, 500 in 2024 and 4, 200 in 2025 coexist with smaller respondent counts. Remote staff abroad are separately disclosed; national domestic-only boundary is not fully documented.
Annual 2015–2024 domestic annual-average full-time positions, with payroll/owner and consultant exclusions. Some late accounts and retrospective cohort exclusions limit literal year-end comparisons.

A government parliamentary answer reports nearly 2,000 games-sector employees in 2021. The text places esports within games, and does not isolate a developer/publisher-only denominator. The previously quoted 2,700 is expected manpower demand, explicitly not an achieved employment count.

TOGED supplies a 2023 employment estimate of 10,777 in the EGDF report. The questionnaire requests FTEs including remote workers abroad, so this is not strictly domestic workplace employment. A much lower 2,500-3,000 secondary estimate cannot be verified in its cited original and remains unplotted context.

TAICCA reports 9,929 employees among 133 responding companies in its 2022 games survey, using public job-board data to fill some missing answers. This is a respondent-company sum with a broad value-chain scope, not a national workforce estimate. The 2023 and 2024 report landing pages were located, but their newer employment tables were not retrieved.

No validated national population total recovered. DOU’s major-company panel includes Ukrainian tax residents working abroad and changes membership; retained as context with selected directly reported company observations.

Periodic ESA firm-mapping estimates cover 2015, 2016, 2019, 2023 and 2025. Core development/publishing can be derived from explicit subsectors for 2019/2023/2025. Broad totals are not a consistent time series; no verified national contractor or foreign-national share was found.

A government news article repeats Vietnam Briefing’s 4,100 workers in 2024, but the underlying article also claims 35,000 developers without reconciling scopes. A 2025 Nhan Dan interview estimates nearly 10,000 people specifically in mobile games. These are conflicting or differently bounded contextual estimates, not a comparable annual national core series.
